intro: LTV:CAC ratio compares what a customer is worth over their lifetime against what it cost to acquire them. Enter your LTV and CAC figures below.

sections.heading: What it measures
sections.body: LTV ÷ CAC, shown as a multiplier. An LTV of $720 against a CAC of $240 gives a ratio of 3.00x — the customer is worth three times what it cost to acquire them, before accounting for how long it takes to actually see that value.

sections.heading: Which LTV number to use here
sections.body: This ratio is only as sound as the LTV figure you feed into it. The simple/historic LTV model (average order value × purchase frequency × lifespan) doesn't account for margin, and plugging it in here will overstate how much room you actually have to spend on acquisition — it's measuring revenue potential, not what the business actually keeps. The margin-adjusted LTV model is the one built for this comparison, since it already factors in gross margin before the ratio is taken.

sections.heading: Reading the ratio
sections.body: A ratio above 1x means the customer is theoretically worth more than they cost — but the ratio alone doesn't say how long it takes to realize that value, which is what CAC payback period is for. A high LTV:CAC with a very long payback period can still strain cash flow even though the underlying economics look healthy on paper.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
items: Feeding the simple/historic LTV model into this ratio instead of the margin-adjusted one, which overstates how much the business can afford to spend on acquisition.
Treating the ratio as the whole picture without also checking CAC payback period - a healthy ratio can still come with a payback period too long for the business's cash position.

seo.seoDescription: Calculate the LTV to CAC ratio, and see which LTV model belongs in this comparison.
